newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Central looks for growth, acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: Australian Central looks for growth, acquisitions.

text.p: Australia's largest credit union, Australian Central Credit Union, said on Thursday changes proposed by the Wallis financial inquiry would allow it to use capital share issues to fund growth and interstate acquisitions.

Australian Central chief executive Sam Walters said restrictions on credit unions' access to capital limited growth to a ratio of profits retained and had forced his organisation to "put on the brakes" on growth in March this year.

"If we could have raised capital by going to our members for further share issues, that would have given us the opportunity to continue our growth and probably pick up another A$30-40 million worth of growth for the year," he told reporters.

Speaking after a business luncheon, Walters said the implementation of the recommendations of the Wallis report into the financial sector would provide that access to growth plus savings of costs in changes to liquidity requirements.
He said Australian Central would not want to be fully listed and would rather be an alternative to the banking system.

Walters said changes in access to capital would allow the credit union, which currently operates in South Australia and the Northern Territory and has an asset base of A$700 million, to cross interstate borders.

Australian Central was most likely to look at mergers or acquisitions of operators with assets from A$100-A$150 million up to its own size, with a geographic focus on Brisbane and Perth or eastern State regional markets, he said.
Walters said the credit union expected its 1996/97 result to improve on the previous year's A$6.2 million net profit, which in that year represented one percent of its assets.
"We targeted to continue that exact same ratio," he said.
However, he said 1997/98 profit growth would be hit by the rise in tax to 36 percent from the current 20 percent rate, given an environment where it must absorb the extra costs.
"While we would still expect to have a successful year that is going to have a significant impact," he said.
As a result, Australian Central would put its focus on cost control this year, and did not plan to open any new branches.
Walters said he expected to see a rationalisation of the credit union industry once the Wallis recommendations were implemented, with the trend already underway in Victoria.
